transcript:
## Christian Nationalism: Properly Defined and Examined

We are looking ahead to our nation's 250th anniversary next weekend. Last week we examined the role of Presbyterians in the American War for Independence. Today, I want us to examine something called Christian nationalism—a term that sounds good on its face since we are Christians and we want to be patriots, and both of those things are good. But there is more to this term than that.

This lesson is particularly important because the term Christian nationalism has become one of the most controversial expressions in American Christianity. For some Christians, it represents a recovery of Christian civilization, a rejection of secular neutrality, and a call for nations to submit to Christ—and these are good things that we would affirm. But for others, it represents racial tribalism, political idolatry, and an attempt to fuse Christianity with political power, which we would reject.

As believing people, as reformed, persevering people, we should resist simplistic answers and strive for more careful theological thinking instead of just adopting a particular term without actually thinking about all the ramifications. Sometimes a term might be good, and yet because of the people who have embraced it, we may want to distance ourselves from it.

The purpose of this lesson is to help us think biblically and confessionally about Christian nationalism. I am capitalizing nationalism here because I am not simply talking about a Christian who loves his or her country—that is not what we are discussing. This is a particular movement: Christian nationalism. We want to avoid both unbiblical nationalism and unbiblical secularism. We do not want a theology of government that does not allow God to be part of it.

## Understanding the Controversy Around the Term

When you hear the words "Christian nationalism," what comes to mind? Common responses include Doug Wilson, Aryan nation, right-wing fundamentalism, theonomy, anger, and focus on this world. I think all of these are common responses, but they are responses that are reviews, not the actual sources. I am not advocating for Christian nationalism, but we have to be careful that we actually know what it says before we reject it. If we are going to reject it, let us do so because we know what it says, not because we read a review, a blog post, or a tweet.

One of the reasons this subject is difficult is that different people mean very different things by the same term. To properly define Christian nationalism, I am going to use the definition of Stephen Wolfe, the man credited with coining the term and writing *A Case for Christian Nationalism*. This is a vetted, traditionally published book, not self-published.

Wolfe defines Christian nationalism this way:

> "Christian nationalism is a totality of national action consisting of civil laws and social customs conducted by a Christian nation as a Christian nation in order to procure for itself both earthly and heavenly good in Christ."

More plainly stated:

> "Christian nationalism is the belief that nations ought to acknowledge Christianity publicly and order their laws and customs according to Christian principles because God enters into covenants with nations and grants them favored status before him."

Intrinsic to Christian nationalism is the idea that God enters into covenant, much like He did with Israel in the Old Testament, and that those nations with whom God enters into covenant have a favored status with God more than any other nation.

## Connection to Theonomy and Postmillennialism

It is very difficult to be a true Christian nationalist without being a theonomist. A theonomist is one who believes that the civil laws found in the Mosaic Covenant should be adopted by governments today—not the ceremonial or sacrificial laws, but the binding civil laws. A theonomist believes those laws should now be adopted and enforced by government.

You cannot be a theonomist without being postmillennial. In order to consistently apply this position, you must believe several things: you have to be a theonomist, and to be a theonomist, you need to be postmillennial. People can be inconsistent, but that is the logical flow if you consistently apply the doctrine. These are the pieces that need to be in place if you want to consistently apply Christian nationalist doctrine.

Additionally, Christian nationalism extrapolates from the Old Testament laws and the relationship God had with Israel, making that a pattern in which God deals with all nations—that what God did with Israel is possible for Him to do with other nations as well.

## Four Distinct Forms of Christian Nationalism

### Cultural Christian Nationalism

The first form says that America has a Christian heritage and we should preserve it. This is something we all favor—as long as we are not favoring cultural Christianity without the work of the Spirit in people's hearts.

### Political Christian Nationalism

The second form is political Christian nationalism, which holds that the state should favor Christianity and Christian morality. What do we think of that? Our confession actually says this. The job of government is to protect the church and the worship of the true God. If you are an elder or deacon in the church, that is what you believe. This is detailed in the Larger Catechism.

The problem is that we always deal with corrupt government—not because government is inherently bad, but because it is made of people, and all of us are corrupt. We have to be very careful about the power given to government to decide what faith should be followed, because depending on who is in power, that might be determined wrongly. This is why our forefathers established a government with three branches of power to try to keep corruption at bay, so that one man or one group of people does not have ultimate power.

### Integralist Christian Nationalism

The third form is integralist Christian nationalism. This holds that not only should the state protect Christianity, but it should actively promote Christianity. This is the Stephen Wolfe kind of Christian nationalism. When you see the term "Christian nationalism" used critically, this is often what is meant. For example, under this view, it should be a capital offense to worship any other god. I am not saying Wolfe explicitly states this, but this is the thinking that follows from that position.

### Ethno-Nationalism

The last form is ethno-nationalism. This is the version that I think most of you have encountered based on the responses given earlier. Some combine Christian identity with ethnicity or race. This category has generated enormous controversy and has caused many Christians to reject the entire movement—and with good reason.

There is a movement called "kin-ism." I first thought it was "Ken-ism," like Barbie's boyfriend, but it is K-I-N-ism. This teaches that the Bible forbids any relationship across ethnic lines. Some conclude that Christian nationalism teaches this. I hope you can see that any idea elevating one ethnicity over another, one look over another, one color over another, is to be rejected scripturally.

## Important Distinctions

Christian nationalism is not simply loving America, displaying the flag, appreciating the founding fathers, or supporting conservative politics. This is simply patriotism. Patriotism is a good thing, but patriotism is not the same as Christian nationalism.

Christian nationalism has become a pejorative word, used to put down anybody to the right of you. "Oh, he is a Christian nationalist. He actually believes the Constitution should be upheld." But that is just patriotism, technically being American. We must make the distinction between patriotism, which is good, and Christian nationalism.

Someone can be a patriotic Christian without being a Christian nationalist. Someone can be a true Christian nationalist and still reject racism or ethnic tribalism. Christian nationalism does not require that. Do not equate Christian nationalism with racism. Yes, one very loud group out there does that, but that is not the whole movement.

## A Biblical Doctrine of Nations

It is important that we have a biblical doctrine of nations and government, that we know what is true and then compare everything else to it.

### God Created Nations

One thing we learn is that God created nations. Acts 17:26 says:

> "And he has made from one blood every nation of man to dwell on all the face of the earth."

This is very important for thinking about the ethnic component. All peoples come from one blood. There are only two races in this world: the race of Adam—that is, every person who has ever lived—and the race of Christ. Either you belong only to the race of Adam, or you also belong to the race of Christ. That is the best way to think about race.

Because God created nations, nations are not an accident or an invention of the human mind. They are part of God's providential ordering of the world.

### God Governs Nations

We also know from the Bible that God governs nations. Daniel 2:21 says:

> "He removes kings and raises up kings. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding."

Psalm 22:28 says:

> "For the kingdom is the Lord's and he rules over the nations."

This is speaking of Christ. No nation is autonomous. No nation escapes divine accountability.

### God Judges Nations

We see in the Bible that God judges nations. We find judgment against Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, and Rome. The first half of Isaiah is pretty much a judgment against one nation per chapter. Nations can be blessed; nations can be disciplined, judged, or destroyed because they are created by God and belong to Him—not because He entered into a special covenant with each one of them. There is a creation relationship, not a covenant relationship, with all nations.

### God Saves People from Every Nation

We also read in the Bible that God saves people from every nation. Revelation 7:9 says:

> "I looked and behold a great multitude, no one could number, from all nations, tribes, peoples and tongues standing before the throne and before the lamb, clothed with white robes with palm branches in their hands."

Christianity is neither anti-national nor nationalist. Christianity is not against nations, but it is not nationalism in the sense of saying that one nation is better than other nations in the sight of God as far as redemption and worshiping the Lamb. The church is multinational.

## A Biblical Doctrine of Government

There is also a biblical doctrine of government. At the core of that is that authority is ordained by God. Romans 13 tells us that civil government is ordained by God, that civil government is a minister of God, and that civil government is an avenger against evil and a promoter of good.

In order to be that, you have to have some sort of standard. You have to figure out what good is. Since Romans 13 is in the Bible and is applicable to every nation on earth at every time, there must be a universal standard of good. We know that is God's law. In some way, God's moral law needs to be the guiding principle that governments, if they are faithful to God, follow in directing the nations.

You might say, "But Tito, I thought you said you are not a Christian nationalist. How can you say God's law should guide governments?" You do not have to be a Christian nationalist to believe that the law of God is supposed to be the guiding principle for all governments on earth. You just have to believe the Bible.

Our confession in chapter 23 says:

> "God has ordained civil magistrates for his own glory and the public good."

Historically, Presbyterians have never been political anarchists. We have not said, "No government." Maybe the Covenanters—"No king but Jesus"—but historically Presbyterians have not been anarchists, and we have not been secularists either, saying, "The government, the Bible has nothing to say about it. We should not be involved with that." The reformed faith has always confessed Jesus Christ as king over nations as well as individuals. There is a role for Christianity in government.

## The Good in Christian Nationalism

There are good things in Christian nationalism, and we need to be aware of them. Many of the concerns raised by Christian nationalists deserve serious consideration.

### There Is No Neutral Society

First, there is no neutral society. That does not exist. Every society has moral commitments, ultimate authorities, and religious assumptions. Secularism—the idea that God is removed from government and society—is itself a religion. Let us not fool ourselves into thinking that such a thing as neutrality exists. Psalm 2 asks, "Why do the nations rage against God and His Messiah?" That is not neutrality.

### Christ Is Lord Over Politics

Another good thing Christian nationalism brings up is that Christ is Lord over politics. Again, in Psalm 2, what are the kings of all nations supposed to do? They are supposed to kiss the Son. All governments are accountable to Jesus. Politics is not outside of Christ's authority. I hope that none of us leave our Christianity at church on Sunday, but that it goes with us on Monday to the public square.

Let me make a statement now: Two kingdoms theology is not biblical. The idea that you leave the Bible outside the public square is not good. Many Christians today in the West subscribe to that. If you disagree, come talk to me.

### Christian Civilization Has Produced Great Blessings

Another thing Christian nationalism rightly brings up is that Christian civilization has produced great blessings. It is better to be a Christian civilization than not. Christianity has elevated all the underclasses. Christianity has been a deliverer for anyone oppressed. Christianity has helped produce hospitals, universities, constitutional governments, abolition movements, care for the poor, and human rights. America's Christian heritage should not be despised.

### Christians Should Seek the Good of Their Nation

One last good thing Christian nationalism brings up: Christians should seek the good of their nation. If you say, "I am just a member of the heavenly city. I have no concern with my earthly nation," you are not being dominated by Scripture. God said to the Israelite captives in Babylon in Jeremiah 29:

> "Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive and pray to the Lord for it. For in its peace, you will have peace."

Even as captives, even as pilgrims in a foreign land, we are to pursue the good of the cities we are in.

## Concerns and Dangers in Christian Nationalism

Now, there are some concerns and dangers that I have with Christian nationalism. There are dangers and excesses, and this is where much of the contemporary controversy lies.

### Confusion of America with the Kingdom of God

Danger one: there is a tendency to confuse America with the kingdom of God. America is not the new Israel. God's covenant nation is not us. We are not necessarily uniquely God's redemptive instrument. God works through other nations and other peoples as well. Who is God's holy nation? The church. In 1 Peter 2, Peter says to the visible church:

> "You are a holy nation."

### Political Messianism

Danger two: the idea of political messianism—that if we can win politically, we can save the country. There is some truth to that. Sure, there is a measure of saving that happens there. But the Bible says:

> "Put not your trust in princes."

Government can restrain evil, but it cannot regenerate hearts. Historically, the church has been at its best when government has persecuted it. Not that we should pray for that, but great times of revivals have happened when the church has been in difficult situations because of political persecution.

### Neglect of the Church's Mission

Another danger: we have become so focused on political change and political campaigning and nationalism that we actually forget and neglect the mission of the church. The church's mission is preaching, discipleship, the sacraments, and discipline. The mission of the church is not national restoration. The mission of the church is not conservatism. There are things we should not conserve. To be a conservative is to say things should not change, that we should conserve things in a certain way. There is much that we want to conserve, but that cannot be our default position because there are things that we do not want to conserve.

### National Idolatry

Danger four: national idolatry. Not that the church in the United States ever struggles with this, right? What do we think when someone says another person is a "God and country" kind of guy? Usually, we mean "country and God" in that order. Christian nationalism has a tendency to become national idolatry. Even our good patriotism can become idolatrous. Any nation can become a false savior. Any nation can become a substitute identity or an object of ultimate hope. We have to guard ourselves against that.

### Ethno-Nationalism and Anti-Semitism

Danger five—and this is the one that produces the most time in news and social media discussions—is ethno-nationalism and anti-Semitism. Why do you think that the definition of Christian nationalism leads some people to anti-Semitism? Because the United States now has the favored status, national status before God. There seems to be an innate need to discredit Israel for that.

Personally, theologically, I do not believe the Bible teaches that today God has any special relationship with the nation of Israel. I do not think the Bible teaches that the nation in Palestine has any special place with God. But there is no need to put them down or be against them as a people for that. In the same way, there is no need for us to blindly support Israel. Either position is not thinking—it is blindness.

I think we would be in a better place if there were no social media. A lot of this stuff happens because cowardly people hide behind computers without facing people face to face, being courageous enough to say things they should not be saying.

Now, some Christian leaders who otherwise share concerns about secularism have distanced themselves from these errors. The Moscow group came up with the Antioch Declaration in which they very clearly denounced racism, ethnic tribalism, and any of that. So good for them for doing that. Not every movement that calls itself Christian is actually operating according to Christian principles, and that is true in a lot of Christian nationalism.

## Why This Matters

Why does this matter? The church has often been tempted by nationalism, racism, tribalism, and political idolatry. The church has also hidden behind a doctrine called the "spirituality of the church." That is what the Southern church did throughout all of the slavery debates. "Oh, we are a spiritual entity. We should not speak into these kinds of debates." That is not what we are furthering here. Sin must be rejected—sins to the left and sins to the right.

Think of it as a road with a ditch on both sides. The ditch to the left is as bad as the ditch to the right, and the ditch to the right is as bad as the ditch to the left. We stay on what the Bible teaches us.

Paul says in Galatians 3:28:

> "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus."

In Ephesians 2, Paul says that the middle wall of separation that divided people ethnically in the Mosaic covenant has been torn down. That is not there anymore.

## How Should We Think About These Issues?

I think it is important that we think biblically, and first of all, avoid a couple of errors.

Error one: we should avoid secularism. That is no religious input or saying by the church to the state. Secularism removes God from public life entirely.

Error two: we should avoid Erastianism. Erastianism is a doctrine that the state is the ultimate saying—it has the ultimate say concerning things in the church. That is not what the Bible teaches either.

We should believe that Christ is king overall. Paul says that God put all things under Christ's feet and gave Christ to be the head over all things and to the church. Not just head of the church, but head over all things. All authority belongs to Christ, so there is no neutral territory.

But God has established distinct spheres: family, church, and state. Each institution has distinct authority, distinct officers, and distinct responsibilities. We have to keep in mind that the church has spiritual authority. The church possesses the word, the sacraments, and discipline. The church does not possess taxation or coercion.
